Look around the room, and illustrate it.

The room takes shape as you turn through it. I'll fix what is here before describing it.The ceiling slopes so low on the left that your shoulder nearly brushes it. The plaster is the color of old tea, cracked along the beam, and the air holds the cold of a room that has not been lived in long enough to warm.

An iron bed takes most of the floor. Its blanket is gray wool, thin at the fold, and the mattress sags toward the wall. At the foot stands a deal table with one leg shimmed by a folded scrap of paper. An oil lamp sits there, glass chimney sooted, wick unlit. Beside it, a washstand leans a little: chipped white basin, a cake of soap gone hard at the edges, a towel stiff on its nail.

The only window is small and streaked with soot. Rain has been at the glass. Through it you make out wet cobbles, a gutter running brown, and the opposite wall of some other building close enough to touch if the sash would open. The street is quiet. Somewhere below, a stove ticks as it cools.

Coal dust ghosts the hearth. A single chair, cane seat frayed, waits under the window as if someone meant to sit and watch the street and then thought better of it. Your own shadow stretches long across the boards when you turn. Nothing else moves. The door, painted the same tired brown as the wainscot, is shut, and the key is not in the lock.
